The Battle of Drepana (249 BC) is another of those Roman wars which military historians find riveting and others find a colorless parade of triremes and blockades. This battle managed to distinguish itself among historians of religion. Roman religion, like much of early religion, had no central text, little philosophy, and few necessary tenets. Reconstructing its practice is a process of collecting and interpreting anecdotes and asides. When Cicero, the orator and philosopher, turns his mind to The Nature of the Gods, historians of religion listen. Historians of religion can be as colorless and tedious as military historians, but not Cicero. You don't become a famed orator if you can't tell a story.

The cultural details you need to know: Before battles, Roman generals made sacrifices and consulted omens. Ever since the second king of Rome, Numa Pompilius, watched the flights of birds, Romans were fascinated by the signs and knowledge of the avian world. If chickens refused to eat before a battle, Romans believed that the bird-brains knew more than they did: today was a bad day to die.

Now, on to Cicero, De natura deorum, 2.3:

Even if we think that the stories of Mopsus, Tiresias, Amphiaraus, Calchas and Helenus are simply tall tales (though their powers of divination would not even have been incorporated in the legends had they been entirely repugnant to fact), shouldn't the instances from our own local history teach us to acknowledge divine power? Should we be unmoved by the story of the recklessness of Publius Claudius in the first Punic War? Claudius mocked the gods merely in jest: when the chickens refused to eat after being released from their cage, he ordered them to be thrown into the sea. "If they won't eat, then let them drink!" he joked but the joke cost him many tears and the Roman people a great disaster, for the fleet was severely defeated. During the same war, his colleague Junius lost his fleet in a storm after failing to comply with the auspices. In consequence of these disasters Claudius was tried and condemned for high treason and Junius committed suicide.

Modern scholars have suggested that this never happened because Polybius makes no note of the story. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Nothing in the story is implausible, nor is the story weighty enough to form the centerpiece of the account of a battle.
